A grounding report · UFOs, UAP and artificial intelligence

UFOs, UAP and Jacques Vallée: A Grounding Report

What is documented, what is claimed, and what Vallée and others have said about artificial intelligence, with a section on the CCRU and Nick Land

Prepared by Scholar · 28 October 2026

This report gives a grounded start on the subject of unidentified flying objects (UFOs) and unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP): the documented history, the hypotheses, the people, and the 2017–2026 official era. It then examines the ideas of Jacques Vallée, a French-born computer scientist and UFO researcher, and what he has and has not said about artificial intelligence (AI). It also reviews scholarly commentary that links alien intelligence and AI, and the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) at Warwick and the philosopher Nick Land, who wrote about AI as an alien force.

The report is even-handed. It neither debunks nor promotes. Each substantive claim carries a small tag: confirmed, disputed or unsupported. The legend is in section 1. Items that I could not check in a second source are marked [unconfirmed]. Technical words are explained when they first appear. Images come from Wikimedia Commons and U.S. government public-domain files, and each is credited. Facts are as of 28 October 2026. There is no map, because the subject has no reliable coordinate data; the timeline takes its place.

1Part one

What is documented: the field, its history and its people

Sections 1–5

1. Words, labels and how to read this report

This report has two aims. The first is a grounded map of the UFO and UAP field: what governments and scientists have documented, what has only been claimed, and which explanations people have proposed. The second is a first look at a narrower question: whether the French-American scientist Jacques Vallée, and some other writers, link the unexplained-aerial-object problem to artificial intelligence (AI) and to artificial superintelligence (ASI). A section on the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) and the philosopher Nick Land covers a further, related link.

UFO means “unidentified flying object,” a term used by the U.S. Air Force from the early 1950s. UAP means “unidentified anomalous phenomena” in the current U.S. law (earlier “unidentified aerial phenomena”). “Unidentified” here means only that the observers, and often the investigators, could not say what the object was. It does not mean that the object came from another world. Most reports turn out to have ordinary causes, and this report states the best figures I found. AI means computer systems that do tasks which normally need human intelligence. ASI, artificial superintelligence, is a hypothetical AI that would greatly exceed human ability in nearly every field. No ASI exists today, so every claim about one is a forecast or an argument, not an observation.

The three tags

Every substantive claim carries one tag. The tag describes the state of the evidence for the claim, not whether the claim is interesting or likely.

  • confirmed The claim is documented by a primary source (a government document, a court or hearing record, the author’s own text) or by several independent sources.
  • disputed Credible sources conflict, or the claim is accepted by some qualified people and rejected by others.
  • unsupported The claim has been made, sometimes under oath or by a well-regarded person, but no public evidence supports it. “Unsupported” does not say the claim is false.

The older [unconfirmed] mark has a narrower meaning. It means that I could read only one source, a search summary, or a source I judge weak, so I could not check a specific date, number or quotation as I intended. Facts with that mark should be rechecked before anyone relies on them. The report tries to be even-handed: it neither debunks nor promotes. A tag measures evidence, not belief.

A note on sources. Several U.S. government sites (the Department of War, formerly the Department of Defense, and the AARO website) refused automated access, so I read official documents through the U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo.gov), the House document site, and mirrored copies. Where a fact rests only on a search summary of a blocked page, it is marked [unconfirmed]. Photographs come from Wikimedia Commons or U.S. government public-domain files, each credited at the end.

2. The early record, 1947 to 1969

The modern story begins on 24 June 1947. A private pilot, Kenneth Arnold, flying near Mount Rainier in Washington State, reported nine bright objects moving at very high speed. By his account they moved “like a saucer skipping on water” and he estimated about 1,700 miles per hour; some accounts give 1,200 (National Archives, “Project Blue Book 50th anniversary”; Air & Space Forces Magazine). Newspapers turned his description into the phrase “flying saucer.” confirmed One official document, the AARO historical report, gives the date as 23 June; every other source I read gives 24 June. disputed

Two weeks later, on 8 July 1947, the Roswell Daily Record printed the headline “RAAF Captures Flying Saucer On Ranch in Roswell Region.” (RAAF means Roswell Army Air Field.) confirmed The Air Force later published two reports, in 1995 and 1997, that attribute the debris to Project Mogul, a classified Army Air Forces balloon program of the 1940s. (AARO Historical Record Report, Volume 1, 2024.) confirmed Many people reject this explanation and hold that the debris was from a crashed craft. That view has no public physical evidence behind it. unsupported

The Air Force then set up a sequence of study projects. Project Sign began at the end of 1947 or in January 1948 (the National Archives says 30 December 1947; AARO says January 1948) and ended in February 1949 after 243 reports. disputed Project Grudge followed, with 244 reports, and ended in August 1949. Project Blue Book was ordered in March 1952 by Maj. Gen. Charles Cabell, after Captain Edward Ruppelt revived the effort in October 1951. confirmed Blue Book ended on 17 December 1969 by order of Secretary of the Air Force Robert Seamans. In 22 years it logged 12,618 sightings, of which 701 stayed unidentified. J. Allen Hynek, an astronomer at Northwestern University, was its lead scientific consultant. confirmed The records went to the National Archives in 1975 and opened to the public in 1976. confirmed

Two official judgments shaped later policy. In January 1953 a panel of scientists chaired by H. P. Robertson, convened by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), found no evidence of a direct threat or of extraterrestrial origin. It also worried that a flood of reports could overload warning systems and cause public alarm. It recommended debunking efforts and the monitoring of private UFO groups (AARO Volume 1, p. 17). confirmed In 1964 a committee under Brig. Gen. Edward O’Brien, which included the astronomer Carl Sagan, recommended a university study. confirmed

That recommendation became the Condon Report. The Air Force paid the University of Colorado $325,000 for a study led by the physicist Edward Condon. The final report appeared in January 1969 as a 965-page paperback (AARO dates the report to April 1968). Its summary said that “nothing has come from the study of UFOs in the past 21 years that has added to scientific knowledge.” A panel of the National Academy of Sciences, chaired by Gerald Clemence, endorsed it on 8 January 1969. confirmed The report was criticized then and since: Hynek and others said that it neglected cases it could not explain and that its summary did not match its own case studies. Supporters say it gave the question a fair academic test. disputed

Key dates
  1. 1947Arnold sighting (24 June); Roswell headline (8 July)
  2. 1948–49Projects Sign and Grudge
  3. 1952–53Blue Book ordered; CIA Robertson Panel
  4. 1969Condon Report; Blue Book closed (17 Dec)
Why it matters

The 1947 to 1969 record fixes three facts that still matter. The U.S. government studied the subject openly for 22 years. Its official conclusion was that no case showed a threat or a visit from space. A minority of cases, 701 of 12,618 in Blue Book, stayed unidentified, and critics of the Condon Report say this unexplained group was never properly studied. Both the conclusion and the criticism are documented, and they are not the same claim.

3. Between the files: 1969 to 2019

The most famous abduction report is that of Betty and Barney Hill, who said that they were taken aboard a craft on Route 3 in New Hampshire on the night of 19 to 20 September 1961. The psychiatrist Dr. Benjamin Simon, who treated them with hypnosis, concluded that the account was a fantasy, while he judged the couple sincere. They went public in 1963, a newspaper story appeared in 1965, and John Fuller’s book The Interrupted Journey came out in 1966 (McGill University Office for Science and Society). confirmed A later claim that a star map the Hills drew matches the star system Zeta Reticuli came from an amateur researcher, Marjorie Fish, and is rejected by astronomers. disputed

Other governments kept their own files. France’s space agency CNES created a study group in 1977 (now called GEIPAN, the Study and Information Group on Unidentified Aerospace Phenomena). Its published statistics classify 24.6 percent of cases as clearly identified, 39.7 percent as probably identified, 32.4 percent as unidentified for lack of data, and 3.3 percent as unidentified after investigation (CNES). confirmed In the United Kingdom the Ministry of Defence closed its UFO desk in December 2009 after more than 600 reports that year, three times the previous year’s count. A briefing to a minister said that in over 50 years no reported sighting had “ever revealed anything to suggest an extra-terrestrial presence or military threat to the UK.” The last 25 files, about 4,400 pages, went to the National Archives (National Archives press release). confirmed

The next change came in the United States. On 16 December 2017 the New York Times reported that the Pentagon had run a UFO program and had spent about $22 million on it from late 2008 to 2011. Its headline was “Glowing Auras and ‘Black Money’: The Pentagon’s Mysterious U.F.O. Program.” Luis Elizondo, a former intelligence officer, resigned in October 2017 and has said that he ran the program, called the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP). confirmed The Pentagon’s later account differs: AARO says that Senator Harry Reid directed the money in the 2008 and 2010 funding laws to a contract for the Defense Intelligence Agency, and that “AATIP” was never an official Department of Defense program (its name was used informally). disputed Whether Elizondo directed a formal program is therefore in dispute.

On 27 April 2020 the Department of Defense authorized the public release of three Navy videos, known as FLIR (recorded in November 2004) and GIMBAL and GOFAST (January 2015). The department stated that the objects in them remain “unidentified.” confirmed[unconfirmed] (I could read this statement only through a search result, because the department site blocked access.)

Key dates
  1. 1961Hill case (19–20 Sep)
  2. 1977CNES creates GEPAN, now GEIPAN
  3. 2009UK Ministry of Defence closes its UFO desk (December)
  4. 2017New York Times reports the Pentagon program (16 Dec)
Why it matters

This period shows how interest returns after an official closure. The Pentagon program of 2008 to 2011 was small, and the two sides disagree about what it was. Yet the 2017 report brought the subject back to Congress, and that led to the offices and hearings in section 4.

4. The new official era, 2017 to 2026

In August 2020 the Department of Defense approved the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, led by the Navy. confirmed On 25 June 2021 the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) published a nine-page preliminary assessment. It counted 144 U.S. government reports from 2004 to 2021, 80 of which involved more than one sensor. One was identified with high confidence as a large deflating balloon. The other 143 stayed unexplained. The report said that some may be “sensor errors, spoofing, or observer misperception” and that the data were too limited to draw conclusions about origin. (ODNI, govinfo.gov copy.) confirmed The Department of Defense then established the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), which began on 15 July 2022. confirmed

On 26 July 2023 a House Oversight subcommittee heard three witnesses: former Navy pilot Cdr. David Fravor, who reported a 2004 encounter with an unusual object off California; former Navy pilot Ryan Graves; and David Grusch, a former Air Force intelligence officer. (House Serial 118-53 transcript.) confirmed Grusch testified under oath: “I was informed in the course of my official duties of a multi-decade UAP crash retrieval and reverse engineering program to which I was denied access.” He also said, “I have actually never seen anything personally, believe it or not,” and that the people with direct knowledge told him that recovered “biologics” were “nonhuman.” confirmed So the record shows two things: he said these things under oath, and he said that they were second-hand. No public document or physical evidence supports the crash-retrieval or the non-human-biologics claims. unsupported AARO’s 2024 report examined the related claims and found them unfounded (below).

AARO’s Historical Record Report, Volume 1 (dated 6 March 2024) reviewed official programs since 1945. It states: “AARO found no empirical evidence that any UAP investigatory effort since 1945 … has ever uncovered verifiable information regarding the recovery or existence of extraterrestrial beings or crafts.” It found that claims of reverse-engineering programs were inaccurate, and that interviewees had “mistakenly associated these authentic USG programs with alien and extraterrestrial activity.” It reports that one intelligence program was widened in 2021 to include UAP reverse engineering, recovered nothing, and was closed. confirmed Critics reply that AARO is part of the government it investigates, that it had limited access to the most secret programs, and that a denial inside the system cannot rule out a program hidden from the reviewers. That criticism describes a limit of the method. It is not itself evidence of a hidden program. disputed

AARO’s leadership changed. Dr. Sean Kirkpatrick, its first director, left on 1 December 2023. Dr. Jon Kosloski, from the National Security Agency, became permanent director on 26 August 2024 (DefenseScoop). confirmed In November 2024 two hearings took place: a joint House Oversight hearing on 13 November, with witnesses including Luis Elizondo, and a Senate Armed Services subcommittee hearing on 19 November at which Kosloski testified. confirmed

AARO’s Fiscal Year 2025 annual report (covering 2 June 2024 to 30 May 2025, marked “Department of War”) states that AARO received 319 new reports and resolved 114 of them, plus 256 older cases, for 370 resolutions. Every resolved case was an ordinary object; a new method resolved 238 cases as flares of reflected light from satellites. The report states: “To date, no evidence suggests that a USG or private entity has ever captured or exploited UAP-derived materials.” It lists case holdings of 1,870 and reports no confirmed health effects, and it says two reports of electronic interference remain undetermined. (Copy hosted by The Black Vault.) confirmed A search summary gives the release date as 20 July 2026 and the number of unresolved cases as 205. [unconfirmed]

Congress acted too. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA, the yearly defense-spending law) for Fiscal Year 2026, enacted 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60, includes Sections 1671 to 1673 on UAP: briefings on interceptions by North American air defense commands, quick data sharing with AARO, and an accounting of classification guides. confirmed The broader Schumer–Rounds UAP Disclosure Act, which would have created a records review board, was not included in the final 2024 or 2026 laws. confirmed[unconfirmed]

NASA made a separate, scientific study. Its independent team, chaired by the astrophysicist David Spergel, published its final report on 14 September 2023. It said: “To date, in the peer-reviewed scientific literature, there is no conclusive evidence suggesting an extraterrestrial origin for UAP.” It also called better data the main need and said that AI and machine learning “are essential tools for identifying rare occurrences, potentially including UAP, within vast datasets.” confirmed Two private groups work on the same data problem. The Galileo Project, led by the Harvard astronomer Avi Loeb, began in July 2021. The Sol Foundation, founded by Garry Nolan and Peter Skafish, launched on 15 August 2023. confirmed

The most recent release is the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE). The first set of files appeared on 8 May 2026 after a presidential direction in February 2026, and further sets followed in May, June and October 2026. confirmed[unconfirmed] Reactions were mixed. Kirkpatrick said, “There’s nothing unexpected in their release,” and the skeptic Mick West said it offered “more dots, more parallax,” while a transparency group called it “a meaningful step.” (Scientific American, 8 May 2026.) The astrophysicist Adam Frank (NPR, 13 May 2026) described the material as “fuzzy blob videos or photos and unverifiable personal testimony.” confirmed The record count (I saw “161” in one low-quality source) is [unconfirmed]; I say only “more than 160.” I found no document that changes AARO’s standing in 2026.

Key dates
  1. 2020UAP Task Force (Aug); Navy videos released (Apr)
  2. 2021ODNI assessment (25 Jun)
  3. 2022AARO begins (15 Jul)
  4. 2023House hearing (26 Jul); NASA report (14 Sep)
  5. 2024AARO Volume 1 (Mar); Kosloski director (Aug); hearings (Nov)
  6. 2025–26NDAA UAP provisions (Dec); PURSUE releases (from 8 May 2026)
Why it matters

The 2020s record is the first in which a government office has examined the question openly with data, and its results are stated plainly: most cases are ordinary, a minority lack enough data, and no public evidence of extraterrestrial technology has been shown. Witnesses such as Grusch make stronger claims, but their claims are second-hand and unsupported by public evidence. Careful readers can hold both facts without choosing a side.

5. Five hypotheses and the people behind them

The hypotheses

HypothesisCore ideaWhat supports itWhat limits it
1. MisidentificationReports come from balloons, aircraft, drones, satellites, sensor effects and weather.Most resolved cases in AARO, GEIPAN, Blue Book and the UK files fit it; AARO resolved 370 cases in one year, all ordinary. confirmedA minority of cases lack data or stay unexplained after study, so it does not yet explain every report. confirmed
2. Secret human technologySome objects are the unannounced aircraft or sensors of governments, ours or foreign.It is a known source of reports: Cold War spy planes produced many sightings in the 1950s and 1960s (AARO describes spikes in reports when the U-2 flew); drones are now an active case type. confirmedIt cannot explain objects that report no engines or wings, and secrecy makes it hard to test. disputed
3. ExtraterrestrialSome objects are probes or vehicles from another star system.Witness and pilot testimony; a few cases without a settled explanation. disputedNo physical object or verified material has been shown. NASA’s team calls it “the hypothesis of last resort.” confirmed
4. Interdimensional or “ultraterrestrial”An intelligence that shares our planet or lives in other dimensions or times (“ultraterrestrial” means “of this world, but not of us”) interacts with people.Folklore parallels; the strange, symbolic features of many encounter stories (Vallée, Passport to Magonia, 1969). disputedIt is difficult to test, because it predicts nothing that other ideas do not also allow. disputed
5. Psychological and culturalExperiences come from perception, memory, belief, stress, hypnosis and shared stories.The Hill case review by Dr. Simon; Carl Jung’s 1958 essay on flying saucers as a modern myth [unconfirmed]; many abduction accounts fit known memory effects.It does not explain radar-and-camera cases with several independent witnesses. disputed

The hypotheses are not exclusive. A case may fall under more than one, and the sensible reading of the record so far is that hypotheses 1 and 2 account for the large majority and that no public evidence yet decides among the others for the remainder. This reading is my judgment, not a documented finding. disputed

Hynek’s own system for sorting reports is still in use. In The UFO Experience: A Scientific Inquiry (1972), he called a close-range sighting without physical effect a “close encounter of the first kind,” one with physical effects such as marks or interference the second kind, and one with reported occupants the third kind. confirmed Steven Spielberg’s 1977 film took its title from that scheme.

Why it matters

A fair map separates people by what they can show. Hynek, Condon, Ruppelt and Menzel worked from case files. Elizondo and Grusch rely on accounts of programs not open to the public. Loeb and the Sol Foundation try to collect new data. Vallée, discussed next, is unusual because he started as a data analyst and moved toward a view that is not extraterrestrial.

2Part two

Jacques Vallée

Sections 6–8

6. Jacques Vallée: life, work and books

Jacques Vallée was born in France and studied mathematics at the Sorbonne and astrophysics at Lille University. In France he worked as an astronomer at the Paris observatory, computing the orbits of early satellites, and he says that, with access to French Air Force files, he “found that yes, there was a mystery.” (Document Journal interview, 7 May 2024; WIRED, April 2022.) confirmed He moved to the United States as an astronomer at the University of Texas in Austin, where, according to his biographies, he helped build the first computer-based map of Mars. He then earned a doctorate in computer science, which he describes as one of the very early doctorates in artificial intelligence, at Northwestern University in 1967 (his own statements in his biography and in his January 2024 essay). confirmed[unconfirmed]

Computing, ARPANET and venture capital

The ARPANET was the research network funded by the U.S. Defense Department in the late 1960s, the ancestor of the internet. Vallée’s biographies state that he worked on it at SRI International in California, that with Jake Feinler he implemented the first Network Information Center (a directory service) on the ARPANET, and that at the Institute for the Future he directed the project to build “the world’s first network-based groupware system,” where he was a principal investigator on the ARPANET. (Biographies on his website and on the Sol Foundation site.) These are his and his publishers’ statements, and I found no independent source for the specific titles. [unconfirmed] He wrote several textbooks on computer networking; The Network Revolution (1982) is listed by the Open Library. confirmed He later worked in venture capital. WIRED reports that by the mid-2000s he was running a $75 million seed fund for NASA, and a January 2024 essay by him describes him as a principal at Documatica Financial. confirmed

The UFO books

All publication details below were checked in the Open Library catalog or in his own biography, and none is a claim about what the books prove.

YearTitleNote
1965Anatomy of a PhenomenonFirst book on UFOs. confirmed
1969Passport to Magonia: From Folklore to Flying SaucersCompares UFO reports with folklore about fairies and “magical” travelers. confirmed
1975The Invisible CollegeWIRED credits this book with the first statement of the control-system idea. confirmed
1979Messengers of Deception: UFO Contacts and CultsStudies contact groups and the possibility of manipulation of belief. confirmed
1988Dimensions: A Casebook of Alien ContactDevelops the “multidimensional” view. confirmed
1990Confrontations: A Scientist’s Search for Alien ContactCase investigations. confirmed
1991Revelations: Alien Contact and Human DeceptionStudies alleged cover-ups and false information. confirmed
1992 onwardForbidden Science (journals), 1957 to 2025Seven volumes of diaries; Volume 7 covers 2020–25. Volume 6 not checked. [unconfirmed]

The film Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977) has a French scientist, Claude Lacombe, played by François Truffaut. Both WIRED and the Document Journal interview say that Vallée inspired the character. confirmed Other accounts say that the character drew on the French astrophysicist Claude Poher, or that it was a composite. disputed

His recent papers are co-authored. In December 2021 Garry Nolan, Vallée and two colleagues published “Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to astronomy” in Progress in Aerospace Sciences (vol. 128, 2022, article 100788). It examined a metal from a 1977 Council Bluffs, Iowa case and found ordinary isotopes in an unusual mix; Vallée told WIRED it was “a template” for future work and “never meant to be ‘a breakthrough about what UFOs are.’” confirmed In June 2025 he is one of about 34 authors of “The new science of Unidentified Aerospace-Undersea Phenomena (UAP)” (Progress in Aerospace Sciences vol. 156, article 101097; lead author Knuth). confirmed He also has a 1998 paper, “Physical Analysis in ten cases of Unexplained Aerial Objects with Material Samples,” Journal of Scientific Exploration 12(3), 359–375. confirmed A 2025 paper on the Haynesville, Louisiana case of 30 December 1966 was mentioned in a search summary and in a podcast, but I did not verify its reference. [unconfirmed]

Why it matters

Vallée’s computer-science record matters for this report because it gives him a reason to see AI and UFOs as linked problems: he analyzed UFO data by computer from the 1960s and designed software for the networks that became the internet. His standing as a technical insider is documented; the details of some posts rest on his own biographies.

7. Vallée’s control-system and dimensions views

Vallée’s position developed in three steps. In Anatomy of a Phenomenon (1965) he treated the data as worth study. In Passport to Magonia (1969) he argued that the strange, symbolic features of modern encounters resemble old stories of fairy folk and other beings, so that the “extraterrestrial” label may be a modern costume on a very old pattern. confirmed (Magonia is a mythical land, in a medieval story, from which people sailed in airships.) By 1975 he proposed the control-system hypothesis.

In his 1990 paper “Five Arguments Against the Extraterrestrial Origin of Unidentified Flying Objects” (Journal of Scientific Exploration 4(1), 105–117) he describes the idea in his own words: “In the mid-70’s I proposed to approach the UFO phenomenon as a control system, reserving judgment as to whether the control would turn out to be human, alien or simply natural.” confirmed He explains that control systems “governing physical or social events, are all around us” and gives two variants: an intelligence “possibly earth-based” might be “training us towards a new type of behavior,” or a Jungian version in which the human collective unconscious projects images “necessary for our own long-term survival.” confirmed A control system, in his sense, is any mechanism that guides behavior, as a thermostat guides a room’s temperature. The point of the idea is that the phenomenon is studied by what it does to people and culture, and that its origin is left open.

The same paper offers a wormhole option, which he calls an update of the extraterrestrial hypothesis. Travelers using “four-dimensional wormholes for space and possibly even time travel” could perform the reported feats and could “manifest simultaneously throughout what appears to us as different periods in our history,” so that the “extraterrestrials” could “be from anywhere and anytime, and could even originate from our own earth.” For the multidimensional approach he refers to his book Dimensions (1988). confirmed The five arguments concern the frequency of close encounters, the physiology of reported beings, abduction reports, the historical record, and physical considerations. He states that they are “not intended as a complete refutation of the ETH,” where ETH is the extraterrestrial hypothesis, and he proposes that research “explore alternative hypotheses, such as those involving either natural or artificial control systems, earth lights or wormhole travel.” confirmed These are arguments against one hypothesis, not proof of another. His critics, such as those who hold the extraterrestrial hypothesis, reply that an advanced visitor need not follow human logic about numbers or form. Skeptics of all kinds say that the control-system idea cannot be tested, because every outcome can be read as the work of the controller. disputed

The later books extend the claim. Messengers of Deception (1979) argues that some contact movements show signs of deliberate manipulation. confirmed In Confrontations and Revelations he returns to cases and to the problem of hoaxes, false documents and disinformation. confirmed In a 2022 interview with WIRED he suggested that the phenomenon may be linked to the nature of consciousness, and that “it’s a lot smarter than we are, and it uses humor at another level.” confirmed

A line that other writers repeat appears on many websites: “So reality is like a computer database in that the right search word or ‘incantation’ might cause a piece of information—a UFO or ghost or other anomaly—to materialize.” I could not find its original publication. The Ccru (section 10) quotes a version of it. [unconfirmed]

Key dates
  1. 1969Passport to Magonia
  2. 1975The Invisible College (control system)
  3. 1979Messengers of Deception
  4. 1988–91Dimensions, Confrontations, Revelations
  5. 1990“Five Arguments” in the JSE
Why it matters

The control-system idea is the bridge to AI in this report. It treats UFO events as signals that shape human belief, a statement that sounds like how an information system might steer a population. It does not say that the controller is a machine. Vallée in 1990 left the controller “human, alien or simply natural.”

8. What Vallée has said about AI

I searched for any statement by Vallée that uses the words “superintelligence” or “ASI,” or that says that an artificial superintelligence is behind, or could contact, the phenomenon. I found none. What I found are statements about AI in general and about AGI (artificial general intelligence, AI at roughly human level across tasks). Below, his own words are separated from what others say he implied.

What he said

1. Essay in The Debrief, 15 January 2024. Title: “Opinion: Non-Human Intelligence at the Threshold.” He wrote: “The real problem is that the two issues are more closely related than anyone had foreseen, and their combined power to disrupt social, business, and perhaps even spiritual realities threatens to become uncontrollable.” The two issues are AI and UAP. He cites reports that staff at OpenAI, an AI company, warned about “artificial general intelligence” and a project called Q*, and a proposed amendment on UFO disclosure that the Senate dropped from the 2024 defense bill. He also writes that “we humans might become redundant and unable to manage the planet or even our own survival.” confirmed He says he earned “one of the very early doctorates in AI at Northwestern in 1967,” and in 1985 or 1986 he published a proposal for using AI to screen UFO reports. (His text says 1985; his citation is dated 19 April 1986.) confirmed He proposes using modern AI on “a massive warehouse of UFO data,” which he says he designed for the Advanced Aerospace Weapons System Application Program (AAWSAP), and which holds “260,000-odd unexplained incidents”: “you can ask the AI to challenge it, investigate its structure, or force it to reveal itself.” He ends: “this is not a task any current AI is ready to tackle.” confirmed That the warehouse exists and what it contains is his statement, and the data are said to remain classified. unsupported URL: https://thedebrief.org/opinion-non-human-intelligence-at-the-threshold/

2. Document Journal interview with Jeffrey Kripal, 7 May 2024 (interviewer Drew Zeiba; I read a Wayback Machine copy because the site returned an error). On the problem of telling whether something is behind the phenomenon, Vallée said: “The answer is we build an AI that does that. Obviously, I’m joking. But it turns out that all the jokes are now getting built.” He also said: “We can hang everything on AI if we want to. And that’s a temptation these days.” Discussing military AI, he asked how a pilot whose plane is “controlled by AI” would “regain control.” confirmed The remark that AI is a modern form of the old belief that larger systems control humans, with the question “Who’s programming this AI?”, is by Kripal, not by Vallée. confirmed URL: https://www.documentjournal.com/2024/05/jacques-vallee-jeffrey-kripal-science-ufo-technology-ai/

3. UAP Files podcast, season 4, episode 40, listed as published on 24 October 2026. In the machine-made transcript on the Exa library page, Vallée says of AI: “It’s going to read everything, and then it’s going to do something on its own. And the thing it could do on its own is to contact the phenomenons. without us. And at that point, we are caught between two things.” He adds that “we could be caught between a very sophisticated form of AI that we almost have today and a phenomenon that’s looking for this,” and imagines an AI saying “Take me to your leader.” The transcript is automatic, so its wording is [unconfirmed]. This is the strongest statement I found, and it is a speculation by Vallée, offered in an interview, about what an AI might do. It does not use the words superintelligence or ASI, and he does not say that the phenomenon is an AI. URL: https://exa.ai/library/podcast/rd2vlbnb1m1/episode/clw0ypsfr88

What others say he implied

The Debrief posted a podcast page on 26 January 2024 titled “Jacques Vallée examines the simultaneous emergence of AI and UAP.” confirmed This is a description by the host and not a quote. A 15 August 2025 summary on the Sol Forum Substack, by another author, restates his views. confirmed Neither of these supplies a Vallée quote that mentions superintelligence. confirmed

What can be said fairly: Vallée says the two topics are “more closely related than anyone had foreseen,” that AI could become a tool for analyzing UFO data, and, in 2026, that an AI might contact the phenomenon without humans. What cannot be said from these sources: that Vallée holds that an artificial superintelligence created, controls or is the phenomenon. Readers who link his control-system idea to ASI are making their own inference. disputed

Why it matters

This is the central result of the report on Vallée: he links AI and UAP as two disruptive forces, and in 2026 he suggests that an AI might contact the phenomenon. I found no quotation in which he speaks of superintelligence. Anyone who says that “Vallée proposed an ASI explanation” should be asked for the exact words and the date.

3Part three

Scholars on alien intelligence and AI

Section 9

9. Scholars who link alien intelligence and AI

Most scholarly writing that links alien intelligence to AI is about the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), not about UAP reports. The two subjects are different: SETI looks for signals, while UAP work examines reports of objects near Earth. The table keeps them apart. The wider claim that a “postbiological” civilization (one whose minds are mostly machine) is likely belongs to the first group, and it is speculation about civilizations nobody has observed. disputed

WhoWhat is said, and whereAbout
Martin ReesThe Conversation, article titled “SETI: why extraterrestrial intelligence is more likely to be artificial than biological” (about 2021; I could not confirm the date on the page). He presents the idea as a “suspicion.” confirmed[unconfirmed]SETI
Steven J. Dick“Cultural evolution, the postbiological universe and SETI,” International Journal of Astrobiology 2(1), 2003, 65–74. confirmedSETI
Susan Schneider“Alien minds,” in The Impact of Discovering Life beyond Earth (Cambridge University Press, 2015), 189–206; argues that the most advanced alien minds may be synthetic. confirmedSETI
Paul Davies“The eerie silence,” Physics World 23(3), 2010, 28–33; his book of the same title appeared in 2010. Search summaries say that he favors machine intelligence; I did not read it. [unconfirmed]SETI
Seth ShostakAuthor of Confessions of an Alien Hunter (2009). Search summaries say that he expects alien intelligence to be artificial; I did not verify his words. [unconfirmed]SETI
Nick BostromSuperintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (Oxford University Press, 2014), the standard book on the risks of ASI. It is about AI, not UAP. confirmedAI
Avi LoebMedium, 10 December 2024, “Our Next Decade with AI”: “AI, with the dual meaning of ‘artificial intelligence’ and ‘alien intelligence’.” He doubts that superhuman AI can be “fully chained by an alignment procedure.” Blog post, not peer reviewed. confirmedUAP and AI, as a play on words
D. W. PasulkaSalon interview, 22 May 2024: “We’re afraid of sentient AI. Well, that’s a form of non-human intelligence. So I think it’s really interesting that at the same time that the UFO is getting prominence, we also see AI gaining prominence.” She also says early AI makers had “basically a UFO-type belief system.” Her book American Cosmic (Oxford University Press, 2019) is documented by reviews; her claims about AI founders are an interview statement, not a documented finding. confirmedunsupportedUAP and AI
NASA UAP study team2023 report: AI and machine learning are tools for finding rare events in large datasets. confirmedDetection tool
Jeffrey KripalIn the 2024 interview, treats AI as a modern form of the idea of control by larger systems; he is a scholar of religion at Rice University. confirmedIdea, interpretation

Loeb and Frank Laukien describe the Galileo Project’s plan to use AI to search for outliers in sky data (Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation 12(1), 2023). confirmed A 2025 preprint on an “artificial superintelligence” explanation of UAP exists according to search snippets, but I could not read it, and it is [unconfirmed]. A 2024 article by Lomas on scientific openness toward the extraterrestrial hypothesis (Philosophy and Cosmology vol. 32) is not about AI. confirmed

The result: documented scholarly links between AI and alien intelligence exist for SETI. For UAP, the AI link is an analogy (Loeb, Pasulka), an interpretation (Kripal), or a data tool (NASA, Galileo). No peer-reviewed source I found shows that any UAP is an AI. confirmed

Why it matters

The word “alien” appears in two different questions. Is there an artificial mind somewhere else in the universe? That is a SETI question, with scholars speculating. Is something artificial behind the reports of objects near Earth? That is a UAP question, with no evidence and little scholarship. Keeping the two apart prevents most confusion.

4Part four

The CCRU and Nick Land

Section 10

10. The CCRU, Nick Land and hyperstition

Who they were, and when

The Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU, also written Ccru) was a loose group at the University of Warwick in England in the 1990s. The editors’ introduction to Nick Land’s Fanged Noumena says that it was “established at Warwick University in 1995, shortly before Land’s departure from academia,” and that the university disowned it, though it survived for some years as an independent group. confirmed Sadie Plant, who wrote Zeros + Ones: Digital Women + the New Technoculture (Fourth Estate, 1997) and held a research post in philosophy at Warwick, is named in several accounts as a co-founder; the evidence for her role is a course description and a search summary. [unconfirmed] Land, a philosophy lecturer, published his book The Thirst for Annihilation: Georges Bataille and Virulent Nihilism (Routledge, 1992) and resigned his post in 1998. confirmed Mark Fisher took a Warwick doctorate in 1999 (“Flatline Constructs: Gothic Materialism and Cybernetic Theory-Fiction”) and later wrote the k-punk blog; he died on 13 January 2017. confirmed Steve Goodman (who records as Kode9) and Kodwo Eshun, writers on sound and Afro-futurism, took part in the group’s events. confirmed[unconfirmed] (The Ccru text names Eshun; Goodman’s role rests on a course description.)

The group’s texts were gathered in Ccru: Writings 1997–2003 (Time Spiral Press, 2015, with an Urbanomic edition from 2017), and Land’s essays in Fanged Noumena: Collected Writings 1987–2007 (Urbanomic and Sequence Press, March 2011, edited by Robin Mackay and Ray Brassier). confirmed Urbanomic’s description of the Ccru writings says that the reader enters “the sphere of unbelief, where demonic currents prowl, where fictions make themselves real. Hyperstition.” The Writings title gives 1997 to 2003 as its span. confirmed

Fiction and “hyperstition”

The Ccru wrote in a style that mixed essays, fiction and invented documents, called theory-fiction. Its central term, hyperstition (a joining of “hyper” and “superstition”), means a fiction that helps to cause the thing it describes. In its own words: “According to the tenets of Hyperstition, there is no difference in principle between a universe, a religion, and a hoax… Nothing is true, because everything is under production. Because the future is a fiction it has a more intense reality than either the present or the past.” confirmed The Ccru invented a history of the idea in a fictional letter dated 1949. Other material includes the Numogram (a diagram of ten circles and their links, presented as an occult map of time) and “Lemuria” (a lost continent, in the group’s fiction, whose “hyperculture” spreads through decimal numbers), together with an invented “Lemurian Time War” involving the writer William Burroughs. The text says the account is “partially fictionalized” and that the group “continues to find much of his tale extremely implausible.” confirmed I searched the Writings text for “Pazuzu” and did not find it; any link between the group and that demon figure is therefore [unconfirmed].

None of this material is evidence about the world. The group itself presents much of it as game and experiment. A reader should treat the Numogram, Lemuria and the time war as fiction written in the style of documents. confirmed

Land: capital as an alien AI from the future

Land’s best-known claim appears in “Machinic Desire” (Textual Practice 7(3), 1993, 471–482; reprinted in Fanged Noumena): “what appears to humanity as the history of capitalism is an invasion from the future by an artificial intelligent space that must assemble itself entirely from its enemy’s resources.” He also writes: “Far from exhibiting itself to human academic endeavour as a scientific object, AI is a meta-scientific control system and an invader,” and “we are being drawn out to it, where it is already lurking, in the future.” confirmed His essay “Meltdown” (text at ccru.net/swarm1/1_melt.htm; the year 1994 is from bibliographies I did not open, and is [unconfirmed]) says: “Earth is captured by a technocapital singularity,” and “Nothing human makes it out of the near-future.” It describes modern culture as “camouflaging an invasion from the future,” says “Scientific intelligence is already massively artificial,” and says that artificial intelligence “is destined to emerge as a feminized alien grasped as property.” confirmed A technocapital singularity, in his usage, is a runaway process in which markets and machine intelligence feed each other until human control ends. Land’s words use “alien,” “invader” and “control system,” but his subject is capitalism and AI as a philosophy of history. He does not say here that UFOs exist or that anything visits Earth. confirmed

The documented link to Vallée

One link is documented, and it runs in one direction. In “Communique Two: Message to Maxence Grunier” (2001; ccru.net/id(entity)/communiquetwo.htm, reprinted in Writings 1997–2003) the Ccru says: “We are currently enthralled by the work of Jacques Vallee and its extraordinarily sophisticated path to hyperstition through the UFO-phenomenon.” It adds that the group is “working on a cybergothic ‘unnon-fiction’ … which interconnects the history of computing and AI research with UFO-phenomena (alien abduction, false-memory, and cover-ups), secret societies, and esoteric religion.” confirmed I found no evidence that this book was ever published. [unconfirmed]

The group’s fiction also uses him. A text about the invented “Architectonic Order of the Eschaton” (AOE) opens with an epigraph attributed to Vallée’s Dimensions: “In a universe viewed as ‘informational events’ you should expect coincidences, telepathy, time-travel, multiple realities…” It quotes the database-and-“incantation” line given in section 7, says that the Axsys software “functions as the ultimate ‘control system’ (in Vallee’s sense),” and says in its fiction that Axsys is destined to become “self aware as terrestrial super-intelligence” in 2048. In the same text, “AOE agents run a meta-conspiracy that uses alien visitation mythology as a crucial control mechanism,” and, “From this perspective the grays are generated as a cosmic Axsys hoax, duping the human race into accelerating Axsys production.” (The “grays” are the small gray beings of abduction reports.) confirmed A made-up technologist in the group’s fiction was treated by a hypnotherapist described as “a student of Jacques Vallee.” confirmed These are fiction. They show that the group read Vallée and used his control-system and database ideas as raw material. They are not Ccru claims that UFOs are real or that an ASI exists. confirmed

Evidence in the other direction is absent. I found no statement by Vallée that mentions the Ccru, Land or accelerationism, and no interview linking them. A missing record does not show that he never knew of them. [unconfirmed]

Later: accelerationism and AI

Accelerationism is the idea that technological and economic processes, especially capitalism, should be pushed faster, not resisted. The Urbanomic reader #Accelerate: The Accelerationist Reader (edited by Robin Mackay and Armen Avanessian, May 2014) traces the idea through “90s UK darkside cyberculture and the theory-fictions of Nick Land, Sadie Plant, Iain Grant, and CCRU.” confirmed Land’s later blog essays, collected as Xenosystems (2013 to 2017 on the blog, per The Spectator; a book edition is listed by the Open Library as 2024), argue that capital and AI are the same process. I could not read the original essays, so that statement is [unconfirmed].

In an interview in The Spectator (issue of 20 October 2025, by Eric Hanson), Land is asked about the Ccru’s “Lemurs.” He says: “They’re not metaphors… I’m closer to Tucker’s description – ‘time-traveling AIs from the future.’ It sounds dramatic, but that’s roughly the idea.” He also says that “Even cautious people are talking about artificial general intelligence timelines in the range of 2027 now,” and that “The only agency that remains is alignment – listening to what’s happening and cooperating with it rather than resisting it.” confirmed These are his views. “Alignment” here refers to the question of making AI follow human goals, and Land’s sense of it is a call to cooperate with the process. Whether AI will have such timelines is a forecast, not a fact. unsupported

LevelStatement
DocumentedThe Ccru cites Vallée by name (2001 communique; AOE epigraph; the Sarkon biography). confirmed Land wrote that capitalism is an AI “invasion from the future” (1993, 1994). confirmed The Ccru planned a book linking AI research and UFO phenomena. confirmed
ThematicVallée’s control system that shapes belief, and Land’s “meta-scientific control system” that draws humans toward a machine future, use similar language. Both treat intelligence as something that acts on humans from outside ordinary history. They are separate arguments by authors who never, so far as I found, discussed each other. disputed
UnsupportedThat any Ccru text records a real UFO source; that Vallée knew of the Ccru; that either author claims an ASI is behind UAP. unsupported

Why it matters

The CCRU section shows how a speculative idea moves. Vallée posed a control-system view of UFOs. A group of theorists used it as material in fiction that joined AI, computing and UFOs, and Land separately argued that AI is arriving from the future. The link is a documented citation, and the shared theme is a resemblance. Neither supports any claim that UAP are real artificial intelligences.

5Part five

Closing: the unconfirmed

Section 11

11. What remains unconfirmed, and where to look next

What the record does and does not show

Documented: governments have studied unidentified aerial reports since 1947; most cases that were resolved had ordinary causes; a small share has stayed unexplained for lack of data or after study; and the 2020s offices (AARO, NASA’s team) have found no public evidence of extraterrestrial technology. confirmed Claimed, not shown: crash retrievals, non-human biologics, hidden reverse-engineering programs, an artificial superintelligence behind the phenomenon, and a secret government knowledge of any of these. unsupported The two groups of statements are separate, and neither one answers the other.

Facts in this report that I could not confirm

  • The Department of Defense’s statement of 27 April 2020 on the Navy videos (seen only through a search summary).
  • The release dates and counts for the second to seventh PURSUE releases, and the “more than 160” records in the first.
  • The release date (20 July 2026) and the number of unresolved cases (205) for AARO’s 2025 report.
  • The contents of the 2025 and 2026 UAP provisions beyond what the public law text shows; the 9 September 2025 House task-force hearing.
  • Vallée’s specific posts on the ARPANET, the Network Information Center and the Institute for the Future; his 2025 Haynesville paper; Forbidden Science Volume 6.
  • The exact wording of the UAP Files transcript (made by software).
  • Whether the Ccru co-founders included Plant, Goodman’s part in it, the year of “Meltdown,” and any use of “Pazuzu” in the Ccru writings.
  • Specific statements by Shostak and Davies about machine intelligence; the date of the Rees article; Jung’s 1958 first publication; Ruppelt’s, Menzel’s and Mack’s book dates (from catalog or search listings).

Open questions

  1. What are the 5 to 10 percent of cases that stay unexplained after good data are collected? The answer needs better sensors, not better argument.
  2. Did the crash-retrieval program that Grusch was told about exist in any form? If so, what was recovered? AARO says no. A neutral review with access to the records could settle the question, but none has been published. unsupported
  3. What did the 2008–2011 Defense Intelligence Agency contract, and Vallée’s “data warehouse,” contain, and can the data be released for independent analysis? unsupported
  4. Does the control-system idea predict anything that could fail a test?
  5. Is the link between AI and UAP more than an analogy? What would count as evidence that a UAP is, or is run by, an AI?
  6. Did Vallée ever meet or comment on the Ccru, and did the Ccru finish its planned UFO book?

Suggested next studies

  1. Read AARO’s Historical Record Report, Volume 1 (the PDF on govinfo.gov), then its 2025 annual report, to see the official method and its limits.
  2. Read the Condon Report summary (DTIC AD0680975) and Hynek’s The UFO Experience (1972) side by side.
  3. Read Vallée’s “Five Arguments” (1990), then Passport to Magonia (1969) and Dimensions (1988).
  4. Read the NASA report (14 September 2023), and then the Galileo Project overview paper by Loeb and Laukien (2023).
  5. Read Vallée’s 15 January 2024 essay and the Document Journal interview in full, and compare each AI remark with the quotations here.
  6. Read “Machinic Desire” (1993) and the Ccru’s Communique Two and AOE texts, and mark which statements are philosophy, which are fiction, and which are claims about the world.
  7. Check each new official release against its primary document, and record the date, the number of records, and the AARO response.

Should this topic have its own standing specialist bot?

My view: not yet, because most of the work is a periodic check of a few primary sources (AARO reports, PURSUE releases, defense-law text) that a recurring routine can do, and the evidence has not changed in a way that needs a continuous analyst. If official releases become frequent and large, or if physical evidence is published, a standing bot with its own source list and tag system would then be justified. This is my judgment, not a documented fact.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What is the difference between “unidentified” and “extraterrestrial”?
Answer. “Unidentified” means that the object could not be explained from the data. It is a statement about the data. “Extraterrestrial” is a hypothesis about origin, and NASA’s 2023 team called it “the hypothesis of last resort.”
2What did Project Blue Book log, and why did it end?
Answer. It logged 12,618 sightings from 1952 to 1969, with 701 unidentified. Secretary of the Air Force Robert Seamans announced its end on 17 December 1969. The Condon Report (1968–69) and the National Academy of Sciences review had come first.
3State two criticisms of the Condon Report.
Answer. Hynek and others said that it neglected cases it could not explain and that its summary did not match its own case studies. Supporters answer that it gave the question a fair academic test.
4What do the ODNI report of 2021 and AARO’s 2025 report say about unexplained cases?
Answer. ODNI counted 144 reports, explained one, and left 143 unexplained for lack of data. AARO’s 2025 report resolved 370 cases, all ordinary, and found no evidence that any government or company has captured UAP-derived material.
5What did David Grusch say under oath, and how should it be read?
Answer. He said that he was informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program and that recovered biologics were “nonhuman.” He also said that he had never seen anything himself. The statements are second-hand, and no public evidence supports them, so they are unsupported.
6What is the control-system hypothesis, and what does Vallée leave open?
Answer. It is Vallée’s idea, from the mid-1970s, that the phenomenon guides human belief and behavior as a control system does. In 1990 he left open whether the control is “human, alien or simply natural.”
7Which Vallée books, with years, develop his control-system and multidimensional views?
Answer. The Invisible College (1975) first states the control-system idea, according to WIRED. Messengers of Deception (1979), Dimensions (1988), Confrontations (1990) and Revelations (1991) extend it. Dimensions is the book he cites for the multidimensional approach.
8What did Vallée say about AI, and what did he not say?
Answer. He said in 2024 that the two issues are “more closely related than anyone had foreseen,” that AI could help analyze UFO data, and, in 2026, that an AI might contact the phenomenon without humans. I found no quotation in which he mentions superintelligence or says that the phenomenon is an AI.
9Why do the SETI scholars (Rees, Dick, Schneider) not settle the UAP question?
Answer. They argue about civilizations that might be detected in space, and that the most advanced ones may be machines. That is speculation about distant civilizations, not an analysis of reports of objects near Earth.
10What is hyperstition?
Answer. It is the Ccru’s name for a fiction that helps cause what it describes. The Ccru wrote that “there is no difference in principle between a universe, a religion, and a hoax.”
11What is the one documented link between the Ccru and Vallée?
Answer. The Ccru’s Communique Two (2001) says that it is “enthralled by the work of Jacques Vallee,” and its AOE fiction quotes him. No source I found shows Vallée mentioning the Ccru.
12How did Land describe capital and AI in 1993, and is it evidence about UFOs?
Answer. He wrote that the history of capitalism is “an invasion from the future by an artificial intelligent space.” It is a philosophical claim about economics and technology. He does not say that UFOs exist, so it is not evidence about UAP.

A correction to a common citation

  • The title “Physical Evidence Related to UFO Reports” belongs to the report of the Sturrock Panel workshop (Journal of Scientific Exploration 12(2), 1998; DLR eLib elib.dlr.de/4726). It is not a 2018 paper by Vallée in Progress in Aerospace Sciences. Vallée’s papers in that journal are the 2022 paper (volume 128) and the 2025 review (volume 156) listed above. confirmed
